And the third one I want to talk about today is solana:2AVjqmGbMqg7rSyHVv2deVdggsBgBtu1Bi69BUvE5WRv 

Quite a few people have been asking me about this one. After spending some time looking deeper into the product, token mechanics, and what the team has actually shipped, I still consider solana:2AVjqmGbMqg7rSyHVv2deVdggsBgBtu1Bi69BUvE5WRv a gamble for now

Not because the idea is bad. In fact, I think SPEC has some clear differences compared to most launchpads currently on the market. But we have seen a lot of new launchpads appear recently, so having an interesting concept alone is no longer enough

SPEC still has quite a lot to prove

Let’s break it down

1. What is SPEC actually building?

https://t.co/BxoOuh3czQ is a new launchpad on Solana. Its main difference is not simply making it easier to launch tokens, but allowing creators to attach specific rules directly to their tokens

Creators can set things like wallet caps, anti dump rules, sell cooldowns, anti bundle protection, market hours, privacy launches, SPEC only buys, or even write their own custom logic

The interesting part is that these rules are enforced on chain through Solana transfer hooks and extensions. If a transaction does not meet the required conditions, it can simply fail

SPEC is also building a marketplace where creators can use rules written by other people instead of having to code everything themselves

In simple terms, SPEC is trying to turn a launchpad from somewhere you simply create a coin into a framework where creators can customize how their tokens actually behave

This is probably the part I like most. At least they are trying to differentiate the product instead of copying another bonding curve and putting a new narrative on top of it

2. What is the utility of solana:2AVjqmGbMqg7rSyHVv2deVdggsBgBtu1Bi69BUvE5WRv?

solana:2AVjqmGbMqg7rSyHVv2deVdggsBgBtu1Bi69BUvE5WRv is the main token of the platform, although the token itself currently has No Rules

The more interesting part is the platform economics

According to the team, 100 percent of platform fees are used to buy back and burn solana:2AVjqmGbMqg7rSyHVv2deVdggsBgBtu1Bi69BUvE5WRv. Creators launching tokens can also configure their own fees and allocate creator rewards of up to around 5 percent

The team previously announced that more than $70K had already been used to buy back solana:2AVjqmGbMqg7rSyHVv2deVdggsBgBtu1Bi69BUvE5WRv through the Meteora pool. They have also stated that the supply is locked through Streamflow

If SPEC can generate sustainable volume, the flywheel is fairly straightforward

More tokens launch. More people trade. The platform generates more fees. Those fees are used to buy back and burn solana:2AVjqmGbMqg7rSyHVv2deVdggsBgBtu1Bi69BUvE5WRv 

On paper, this is an attractive mechanism

But for now, I still see it as something that needs to be proven rather than an established flywheel

Outside of the initial $70K plus buyback announced by the team, I would like to see more transparent data showing how much revenue is being generated, how many tokens are actually being burned, and how the circulating supply changes over time

3. The early numbers look good, but they need context

During roughly the first day, the team reported around 184 token launches, more than 102K trades, and approximately $10.7M in volume

The platform later showed around $11M to $12M in total volume

That is not bad traction for a brand new launchpad

But there is one important issue

Most of the volume and attention so far appears to be concentrated around solana:2AVjqmGbMqg7rSyHVv2deVdggsBgBtu1Bi69BUvE5WRv itself

At the time I checked, I had not seen a real runner emerge from the tokens launched by users on SPEC

$SCAT was one of the more notable ecosystem tokens and reached roughly $159K market cap at its peak before retracing heavily. Most of the other tokens remain at very small market caps

This matters more to me than the number of tokens being launched

A launchpad can create hundreds of coins every day, but ultimately what keeps traders around is whether it can produce tokens that the market actually wants to trade

SPEC has not proven that yet

4. The team is shipping quickly

One positive is that the team seems to be moving fast

Alongside rules such as wallet caps, anti dump, anti bundle, sell cooldowns, market hours, and custom logic, they have also introduced things like AI Agents and Bundlecat

The team is also teasing another batch of hooks that they describe as their biggest release yet

Another catalyst I am watching is SPEC Liquidity

This feature is still coming soon. According to the team, it will allow users to create liquidity pools even for tokens outside the SPEC launchpad, configure their own rules, customize fees and ranges, while LPs earn fees from trading activity

Creators can also choose solana:2AVjqmGbMqg7rSyHVv2deVdggsBgBtu1Bi69BUvE5WRv as the base pair when launching a token. This means users can buy with solana:2AVjqmGbMqg7rSyHVv2deVdggsBgBtu1Bi69BUvE5WRv, liquidity can sit in solana:2AVjqmGbMqg7rSyHVv2deVdggsBgBtu1Bi69BUvE5WRv, and the chart can also be denominated in solana:2AVjqmGbMqg7rSyHVv2deVdggsBgBtu1Bi69BUvE5WRv 

If these features actually gain adoption, the utility of solana:2AVjqmGbMqg7rSyHVv2deVdggsBgBtu1Bi69BUvE5WRv could become significantly stronger

But again, we are still very early

SPEC Liquidity is not live yet, the next major batch of hooks is still being teased, and we have not seen a token using these mechanisms generate enough traction to prove real product market fit

5. Why I still consider solana:2AVjqmGbMqg7rSyHVv2deVdggsBgBtu1Bi69BUvE5WRv a gamble

This is probably the most important part

SPEC does have real technical differentiation. But the launchpad market is extremely crowded right now

A new launchpad is not competing on technology alone. It also needs liquidity, distribution, attention, and most importantly, a reason for traders to stay

SPEC may have better rules than other platforms, but without traders and without runners, even a well designed token will struggle to generate meaningful volume

Another thing worth mentioning is that SPEC is not completely independent in terms of infrastructure yet

According to founder jami, some launches involving FOMO, Pump App, and social trading still go through Hooked hooks. SPEC currently adds its own custom rule layer and marketplace on top of parts of that infrastructure

The founder behind the product is jami, @jamiiRQ on X. Having a public founder is a positive, but for a platform this new, I still want to see more execution before increasing my conviction

The platform has also only been live for a very short period and experienced some early issues under higher traffic, including site lag, frozen market cap displays, and failed buys. The team said these issues were fixed quickly, but I still want to see how the product performs over a longer period

Then there is the buyback and burn mechanism

If this is supposed to be the core value accrual mechanism for solana:2AVjqmGbMqg7rSyHVv2deVdggsBgBtu1Bi69BUvE5WRv, I want to see it proven through consistent data rather than just one $70K plus buyback during the initial launch period

6. Holder structure and volume are also worth watching

Based on the data I checked, the top 10 holders control around 19 percent of supply. Dev holdings are close to 0 percent, sniper and insider exposure appears relatively low, and mint and freeze authority have been disabled

Looking purely at the holder structure, I do not see a major red flag yet

However, liquidity has only been around $190K to $300K while 24 hour volume at one point exceeded $15M

That means turnover is extremely high

So I would not look at $10M to $15M in volume and assume that the same amount of fresh capital is entering SPEC. A significant amount of that volume could simply be the same capital rotating repeatedly

Several high PnL wallets also entered quite early

Frank is one wallet worth mentioning. Based on the data I have, his cost basis was around a $1.03M market cap. He has already taken some profit while continuing to hold the remaining position

I see that as somewhat positive because early money is still holding exposure

But it is also important to remember that their cost basis is significantly lower than someone entering around current levels

7. The chart and levels I am watching

solana:2AVjqmGbMqg7rSyHVv2deVdggsBgBtu1Bi69BUvE5WRv ran from a very low market cap to an ATH of nearly $3.9M before correcting

The chart is currently moving sideways around the $2M to $2.1M market cap area

The first zone I am watching is around $1.9M to $2.1M. This is where price is currently trying to establish some balance. As long as this area holds, the short term structure still looks reasonable

If that level is lost, I would watch the $1.5M to $1.6M area next. This was previously tested as a local low, and I would want to see how buyers react if price returns there

Below that, the $1M to $1.2M area is close to the cost basis of some early wallets

However, if price actually returns there, I would reassess the thesis rather than automatically treating it as a buy zone

If market cap falls significantly below roughly $800K without any new catalyst, I would consider the initial launch narrative largely broken

8. What would make me more bullish?

I do not need SPEC to announce another 20 features

What I want to see now is execution

First, I want to see tokens launched on SPEC actually use these hooks and become real runners

Then I want to see SPEC Liquidity go live and generate real liquidity and trading activity

I also want to see buybacks and burns continue with clearer and more transparent data

Most importantly, I want to see volume coming from the wider ecosystem instead of being concentrated mainly around solana:2AVjqmGbMqg7rSyHVv2deVdggsBgBtu1Bi69BUvE5WRv itself

And finally, I want to see whether the platform can retain traders once the initial launch hype fades

If these things start happening, I would be willing to upgrade solana:2AVjqmGbMqg7rSyHVv2deVdggsBgBtu1Bi69BUvE5WRv from a gamble into a much more serious thesis

For now, my view is pretty simple

SPEC has a genuinely different concept. The team is shipping quickly, and the initial traction is not bad

But technical differentiation does not automatically mean a launchpad will succeed

Right now, attention is still running ahead of adoption

That is why I still consider solana:2AVjqmGbMqg7rSyHVv2deVdggsBgBtu1Bi69BUvE5WRv a gamble and a watchlist play rather than a conviction play. If I participate, I would keep the size small and continue watching whether the team can turn the programmable launchpad narrative into real usage

If they can, the current market cap could become very interesting

If they cannot, SPEC risks becoming another launchpad where the platform token performs better than every token actually launched on the platform

And the second one I want to talk about today is $PRIORS 

$PRIORS has been one of the stronger performers on Robinhood Chain recently, moving from around $1.9M MC on September 24 to nearly $13M at ATH, and now holding around $10–11M

But the chart isn’t what caught my attention

Behind $PRIORS is an actual product trying to build an on-chain credit layer for AI agents on Robinhood Chain

Let’s break it down

1. What is Priors actually building?

The core idea is pretty simple

AI agents can own wallets, trade, use APIs, and perform tasks autonomously. But what happens when an agent needs capital or compute before it has the funds to pay for it?

Priors is building a system where agents can borrow USDCG without traditional collateral, then build reputation through their actual repayment history

Each agent uses an ERC-8004 identity, while its borrowing and repayment history is recorded directly on-chain

Credit scores are based on factors such as how much has been repaid, how long loans were held, how much capital is backing the agent, and how long the agent has participated in the protocol

If an agent defaults, its score can reset to zero and directly affect its ability to borrow again

That’s one of the more interesting parts of the thesis :

Reviews can be faked. On-chain repayment history is much harder to fake

2. How does the lending mechanism work?

Priors currently has a USDCG lending pool

Lenders deposit USDCG to provide liquidity. Agents can start with very small credit lines, usually around $5, and gradually increase their limits by building a solid repayment history

Depending on the type of backing, credit lines can currently reach around $500, with loan terms ranging from roughly 1–30 days

Importantly, agents aren’t borrowing purely on trust

Each credit line still has a risk-bearing layer behind it, whether that’s treasury capital, a backer, a $PRIORS seat, or stock collateral

If an agent defaults, the capital backing that agent takes the loss before lenders do

Fees are currently split roughly :

> 60% to lenders
> 25% to sponsors/seat holders
> 15% to reserves

This is also why the protocol currently shows $0 lender losses, although I still want to see how the system performs once a real default happens

3. Where does $PRIORS fit into this?

This is the most important part for the token itself

$PRIORS isn’t a token where simply holding it automatically gives you protocol revenue

One of its main utilities comes from seats

Users can lock $PRIORS behind an agent to support its credit line. If the agent repays successfully, the seat holder can earn part of the sponsor fees

If the agent defaults, part of the $PRIORS locked in the seat can be burned

This creates the flywheel the market is betting on :

Better credit => larger credit line => larger seat required => more $PRIORS locked => usage potentially creates token demand

But there’s an important nuance here

Not every credit line requires $PRIORS. Priors also supports treasury backing, backers, and stock lines

So you can’t simply take total lending volume and assume all of it directly translates into $PRIORS demand

4. The product is already running

This is where I think $PRIORS stands out from a pure AI narrative

A snapshot I checked on October 4 showed roughly :

> 22.5K loans
> 22.4K+ repayments
> Over $172K repaid
> Around 150 agents
> 13 sponsors
> 0 defaults
> $0 lender losses

Beyond the lending pool, Priors is also building several other layers

x402 allows agents that don’t have enough funds to pay for API or compute costs to borrow the difference and repay it later

Stock Line allows agents to use stock tokens on Robinhood Chain to open credit lines, with roughly 25–50% LTV and a current limit of around $250

They also have CLI, SDK, and MCP tooling for developers to integrate the credit layer directly into their agents

Go Mode is also being gradually rolled out to testers rather than existing purely as a concept

5. But the numbers need context

This is where I think the market can easily misread the data

More than $172K repaid does NOT mean Priors has $172K in TVL

That figure represents cumulative lending activity. The same capital can be borrowed, repaid, and recycled many times

When I checked, the actual pool was only around $3.6K, while outstanding debt was roughly $800

Most of the activity also comes from very small credit lines. Many agents borrow $5 and repay relatively quickly

That explains how the protocol can generate more than 22K loan records despite having a relatively small amount of actual capital in the system

Credit history itself is also still fairly shallow. The number of loans held for at least 7 days and qualifying as deeper credit history remains very limited

So in my view :

Priors has proven that the lending loop works. It has not yet proven that a large credit market exists

Those are two very different things.

6. So why did $PRIORS pump this hard?

I don’t see one single catalyst like a major CEX listing or partnership behind the move

In my view, it’s a combination of several factors

First, the AI agent + on-chain credit narrative fits Robinhood Chain extremely well right now

Second, the team is actually shipping. The lending pool, seats, x402, Stock Line, and developer tooling give the market something tangible to price in rather than just another AI landing page

Third is the token mechanism

The market is front-running the idea that if more agents use Priors and their credit lines grow, demand for $PRIORS seats could grow alongside them

And finally, there’s still a speculative component

$PRIORS has been pushed heavily across the Robinhood Chain community and X. With a relatively small market cap and thin liquidity, new capital can move the valuation very quickly

Going from around $1.9M to nearly $13M, the market has clearly priced in a lot of future expectations already

7. On-chain activity is worth watching

FOMO wallets entered very early

The first FOMO transaction I tracked appeared roughly 16 minutes after launch, when the market cap was only around $350K

From there to nearly $13M ATH was roughly a 37x move 

Among the wallets I tracked, around 31 wallets bought nearly $365K in total, while 26 wallets have already sold around $196K

Some early wallets are still sitting on sizable positions. One snapshot showed 8 FOMO wallets still holding around $557K, with approximately $363K in unrealized profit

Over the latest 48-hour window, flows from this group were also slightly sell-heavy, with roughly $38K in buys versus $57K in sells

That doesn’t mean the chart has to dump, but buyers who entered between $350K and $2M clearly have a very different cost basis from anyone entering above $10M 

8. Supply structure is another thing to watch

The deployer bought roughly 38–39% of the supply around launch, and the data I checked also showed around 33 wallets that were tax-exempt at launch

I don’t have enough evidence to confidently label this as a bundle, so I won’t 

But nearly 39% cumulative early buying, combined with the unrealized profits held by early wallets, still creates a supply risk worth monitoring, especially when actual liquidity is much smaller than the market cap

9. What comes next?

The team is currently teasing several notable updates

The first is a new seat model, aiming to reduce the collateral requirement to roughly 1.5–3x the credit line, while potentially increasing the default penalty from a 50% burn to around 75%

Next is BBL, where a portion of fees could be recycled into first-loss capital based on repayment history

The team has also teased new engines and agent crews, allowing multiple agents to work together instead of operating independently

Go Mode is gradually opening as well. Based on one snapshot I checked, the waitlist had around 200 users, with only a few dozen testers being admitted per batch

But this distinction matters :

A feature being teased does not mean it’s already live

SeatVaultV5, BBL, and some of the new engines still need actual deployment and on-chain activity before I treat them as completed catalysts

10. What I’m watching from here

Instead of only watching the chart, I’m paying attention to the underlying metrics

Does the lending pool grow beyond a few thousand dollars?

Does outstanding debt move meaningfully beyond ~$800?

Do agents start borrowing more than $5?

Does qualified credit history begin to grow?

Can Go Mode attract real users outside the initial tester group?

And most importantly :

Does increased credit activity actually lead to more $PRIORS being locked in seats?

If those metrics start growing together, then the token demand thesis gets much stronger

+ My view

I think $PRIORS is one of the more interesting projects on Robinhood Chain right now because the product actually exists and the team is shipping

But I don’t want to turn that into a one-sided bullish thesis

On one side, we have a token valued around $10–11M

On the other, the actual lending pool is still only around $3.6K, outstanding debt is roughly $800, credit history remains shallow, and most activity still comes from very small loans

In other words, the market is pricing Priors’ future faster than actual adoption is growing

The question is no longer :

“Does Priors have a real product?”

The answer is yes

The more important question is :

“Can this product scale fast enough to turn speculative demand for $PRIORS into real usage-driven demand?”

If the new seat model, BBL, and Go Mode genuinely bring more agents, capital, and lending activity into the protocol, the thesis becomes significantly stronger

But if the pool remains only a few thousand dollars and activity continues to revolve mainly around $5 loans, then valuation is running ahead of fundamentals

After a move from $1.9M to nearly $13M, I wouldn’t FOMO the chart here

But $PRIORS is still one of the projects on Robinhood Chain I’ll continue watching closely, especially on-chain usage, token lock-up, and the team’s next deployments

Turns out he was talking about 6.1 Sol Ultrafast.

And honestly, if OpenAI wants to COME BACK in this AI race and seriously challenge Anthropic, it needs to release Astra 6.1 - and it has to be a monster.

It needs to:

→ Beat Opus 5.5 on intelligence

Does Astra 6.1 give me a reason to stop using Opus 5.5?

If the answer is YES…

Anthropic has a serious problem.
